ledger.note: 1235: the duchy is created. 'In 1235, Otto I was enfeoffed with the newly founded Duchy of Brunswick-Lüneburg at the Court of Mainz.' Otto the Child received it in exchange for his estates; the page names no land.

region.text: the Welf estates round Brunswick and Lüneburg

ledger.note: 1370: the Lüneburg war begins. The war 'broke out in 1370 in north Germany and lasted, with interruptions, for 18 years': the Welf Duke Magnus II against the Ascanians of Saxe-Wittenberg (Albert and Wenceslas, backed by Charles IV's enfeoffment); the city of Lüneburg sided with the Wittenbergs and destroyed the ducal castle on the Kalkberg (1 February 1371 per the Lüneburg page).

region.text: the Principality of Lüneburg: Lüneburg, Celle, Hanover and Winsen an der Aller

ledger.note: 28 May 1388: Winsen an der Aller. 'On 28 May 1388, battle was joined at Winsen an der Aller; it ended in victory for Henry' (a Welf); the Peace of Hanover of 1373 had ended the war 'for the time being' and the 1389 inheritance treaty 'finally secured' the principality for the Welfs. The page is inconsistent about 1373 and 1374.

1519: the Hildesheim Diocesan Feud. The conflict 'broke out in 1519'; Hildesheim, with Henry the Middle of Lüneburg and the counts of Schaumburg, Diepholz and Hoya, beat the Welf principalities of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel and Calenberg at the Battle of Soltau on 28 June 1519. Lüneburg was on Hildesheim's side, so only the Wolfenbüttel and Calenberg parts of this state fought.
13 May 1523: the Quedlinburg Recess ends the feud, the 'last medieval feud'; field peace had been made on 15 October 1521.

13 May 1523: the Welfs take the Great Stift. 'Hildesheim was left with 4 of its 22 Ämter, plus the towns of Hildesheim and Peine, and the Kleines Stift'; 'Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel gained many Ämter, abbeys, and towns'; 'Calenberg received fortified seats, Ämter, towns including Dassel and Bodenwerder, half of Hameln, and several abbeys.' Hildesheim 'had won militarily, but lost politically'. The extent is the researcher's reading.

ledger.note: 1584: Diepholz. Calenberg 'acquired Diepholz in 1584' (the same year Calenberg-Göttingen fell back to Wolfenbüttel after Eric's death).
1643: the Main Treaty of Hildesheim. 'In 1643, the Main Treaty of Hildesheim returned most of the lost territories, though some Ämter stayed with Calenberg and Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel.'

1692: the Calenberg line is made elector ('Ernest Augustus acquired the right to be a prince-elector as the Prince-Elector of Brunswick-Lüneburg'); 'The old Principality of Calenberg thus adopted the new name of Electorate of Hanover'. This dossier is not dissolved: it continues as the Welf land outside the electorate, Wolfenbüttel and (to 1705) Lüneburg.

1692: Calenberg and the lands joined to it become the Electorate of Hanover. Principality of Calenberg page: 'Ernest Augustus was rewarded ... with the title of the ninth electorate'; Göttingen merged with Calenberg in the 1400s, Grubenhagen 'was also finally added to the Calenberg dynasty' (1665), 'In 1584 Calenberg also acquired the Diepholz', in 1582 'the larger part' of Hoya. Lüneburg and Wolfenbüttel stay out (Brunswick-Lüneburg page).

region.text: Calenberg-Göttingen, Grubenhagen, the Hameln-Dassel seats, Hoya and Diepholz

ledger.note: 1705: Lüneburg joins the Electorate. Calenberg page: 'In 1705 it was enhanced further by the inheritance of the Principality of Lüneburg'; the Brunswick-Lüneburg page: the dynastic union 'did not occur until 1705 under his son George I Louis'. The electorate-of-hanover dossier records the gain with counterpart principality-of-luneburg, which this dossier carried until 1705.

1807: the Wolfenbüttel line loses its independence. Brunswick-Lüneburg page: 'The Wolfenbüttel Line retained its independence, except from 1807 to 1813'; Duchy of Brunswick page: 'The Wolfenbüttel principality had from 1807 to 1813 been held as part of the Kingdom of Westphalia' and the Congress of Vienna 'turned it into an independent country as the Duchy of Brunswick' (a later state; Cliopatria's Duchy of Brunswick starts 1814). The Brunswick-Lüneburg infobox ends 1806 ('The end of the Holy Roman Empire'); the pages' 1807 is used because the Wolfenbüttel line was independent to then.

wars.name: War of the Lüneburg Succession
wars.outcome: The Peace of Hanover (1373) ended it 'at least for the time being'; the Welf Henry won at Winsen an der Aller on 28 May 1388 and the 1389 inheritance treaty 'finally secured' the principality for the Welfs.
wars.note: The page does not say which towns the Wittenbergs held; its text puts Lüneburg city on their side.

wars.name: Hildesheim Diocesan Feud
wars.outcome: Hildesheim won the Battle of Soltau (28 June 1519, about 3,500 Welf dead, Eric of Calenberg captured) but lost politically; the Quedlinburg Recess of 13 May 1523 gave the Great Stift to Wolfenbüttel and Calenberg; the Main Treaty of Hildesheim returned most of it in 1643.

certainty.note: The pages give principalities, towns and Ämter, not boundaries; the only dated frontier changes are the 1523 Recess and the 1643 treaty. The internal divisions are not drawn. After 1692 only the Wolfenbüttel line (and Lüneburg to 1705) is drawn, a soft circle.

notes:
Written 2026-10-25 for batch eu-09-x (5 pages opened; budget 5). New state: Cliopatria has no Brunswick-Lüneburg row; the Welf lands sit inside Holy Roman Empire Minor States.

WHAT THE STATE IS. The Duchy of Brunswick-Lüneburg (1235) was divided into 'subordinate principalities' under one dynasty: Brunswick (later Wolfenbüttel) and Lüneburg (Celle) 1267/1269 (Lüneburg page; the Duchy page says 1269), Grubenhagen 1291-1596, Göttingen 1345 (the Duchy table gives 1291-1463 elsewhere), Calenberg 1432, Harburg 1527, Gifhorn 1539, Dannenberg 1569, and reunions (Grubenhagen to Lüneburg 1617; Calenberg-Göttingen under Wolfenbüttel 1584-1634, independent again 1635). They are drawn here as one state with one colour, as the Duchy page does (infobox area 21,170 km2 for 1635); the internal divisions are not ledger events because no land crosses the outer border. If the orchestrator wants the principalities as states, principality-of-luneburg and principality-of-brunswick-wolfenbuttel are the natural slugs and the electorate-of-hanover dossier already names principality-of-calenberg and principality-of-luneburg as predecessors.

SHAPES are circles (gazetteer lacks the towns): Brunswick 10.52E 52.27N 35 km; Lüneburg 10.41E 53.25N 42 km; Celle 10.08E 52.62N 38 km; Hanover/Calenberg 9.73E 52.37N 30 km; Göttingen 9.93E 51.53N 30 km; Einbeck/Grubenhagen 9.87E 51.82N 25 km; Hoya (Nienburg) 9.20E 52.64N 25 km; Diepholz 8.37E 52.61N 20 km; Hameln-Bodenwerder 9.45E 52.03N 18 km; the Hildesheim ring 9.95E 52.15N 28 km minus 8 km. Gazetteer names wanted: 'Brunswick' and 'Lüneburg' if absent, 'Celle', 'Einbeck', 'Nienburg', 'Diepholz', 'Hameln', 'Bodenwerder', 'Hildesheim' (as radius places).

NOT SETTLED. (1) The first-year extent of the duchy: the page names no land. (2) Division dates: 1267 or 1269. (3) The Peace of Hanover is 1373 in most places and 1374 in one. (4) The Wittenberg rule: the Lüneburg War page gives no period (the Duchy page has them ruling the principality 1373-1388). (5) Hoya: only 'the larger part' went to Calenberg in 1582; who took the rest is not on the page; Diepholz 1584 on this page, 'earlier-acquired' on the Hanover page. (6) The Great Stift as a ring is a stand-in; which Ämter stayed after 1643 is not given. (7) Thirty Years' War occupations (Danish, Imperial, Swedish) are not entered: no page opened dates them. (8) Dissolution 1692: Lüneburg joined the electorate only in 1705 and Wolfenbüttel stayed apart to 1806; the page's Hanover successor is therefore partial.

COUNTERPARTS NEEDING DOSSIERS: electorate-of-saxony (Ascanian, to 1422), prince-bishopric-of-hildesheim, county-of-hoya, county-of-diepholz, principality-of-luneburg (to 1705), principality-of-brunswick-wolfenbuttel (to 1806/1814), principality-of-grubenhagen (1291-1596).

REVISION 2026-10-25 (after review). The 1692 dissolve into electorate-of-hanover handed over all six Welf circles, but the page says 'The old Principality of Calenberg thus adopted the new name of Electorate of Hanover', Wolfenbüttel 'remained separate' and Lüneburg joined only in 1705 (electorate-of-hanover's own 1705 gain). The dossier therefore continues: 1692 loss of Calenberg-Göttingen, Grubenhagen, the Hameln-Dassel seats, Hoya and Diepholz to electorate-of-hanover; 1705 loss of Lüneburg; the rest is the Wolfenbüttel line to 1807, when it joins the Kingdom of Westphalia (Brunswick-Lüneburg page 'except from 1807 to 1813'; Duchy of Brunswick page 1807-1813). The first note said Wolfenbüttel 'stayed apart to 1806'; the Brunswick-Lüneburg infobox ends 1806 ('The end of the Holy Roman Empire') while its text and the Duchy of Brunswick page give 1807; 1807 is used. The Calenberg circle is cut from the Wolfenbüttel and Lüneburg circles after 1692 (overlap). Counterparts: kingdom-of-westphalia (Cliopatria 1809..1813, no dossier yet); principality-of-luneburg is no longer a successor (its land is carried here to 1705; electorate-of-hanover's gain names that slug as counterpart, not this dossier, and should be changed to duchy-of-brunswick-luneburg); the Duchy of Brunswick (1814 on) needs its own dossier (eu-20). The page 'Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel' does not exist (url_not_found).
